meta.about: Long-term health effects linked to regular excess intake of a nutrient or ingredient type. Wording is deliberately 'linked with' — a single product does not cause a disease. Evidence levels: strong = consistent trials/cohorts and WHO/IARC consensus; moderate = consistent observational evidence; limited = early or mixed evidence.

links.title: Too much salt
links.effect: Regularly eating more than 5 g of salt a day raises blood pressure, which over years increases the risk of heart disease, stroke and kidney damage.

links.title: Too much sugar
links.effect: High intake of free sugars is linked with weight gain and tooth decay, and, through weight gain, with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes. Excess sugar and calories also contribute to fatty liver.
links.source: WHO — Guideline: sugars intake for adults and children (2015)

links.title: Sugar-sweetened drinks
links.effect: Regular sugary drinks are one of the clearest dietary links to weight gain, type 2 diabetes and tooth decay, because liquid sugar does not make you feel full.

links.title: Too much saturated fat
links.effect: Regularly eating more saturated fat than recommended raises LDL ('bad') cholesterol, which is linked with a higher risk of heart disease.

links.title: Trans fat
links.effect: Industrial trans fat raises bad cholesterol and lowers good cholesterol; it is strongly linked with heart attacks and early death from heart disease.

links.title: Ultra-processed food
links.effect: Diets high in ultra-processed foods are linked in large observational studies with obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, depression and earlier death. This shows strong associations, but the exact causes are still being studied.
links.source: BMJ (2024) umbrella review of ultra-processed food and health

links.title: Processed meat with nitrites
links.effect: IARC classifies processed meat as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1): each 50 g eaten daily is linked with about an 18% higher risk of bowel cancer.
links.source: WHO/IARC — Q&A on the carcinogenicity of red and processed meat

links.title: Refined, low-fibre food
links.effect: Diets built on refined grains and low in fibre are linked with bigger blood-sugar swings, constipation and a higher long-term risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease and bowel cancer than diets rich in whole grains and fibre.

links.title: Non-sugar sweeteners
links.effect: WHO advises against using non-sugar sweeteners to control weight: they do not help long term, and observational studies link regular use with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease (low-certainty evidence).

links.title: Synthetic azo colours
links.effect: A UK study found mixtures of some synthetic colours increased hyperactivity in some children. The EU requires a warning label on foods containing them.

links.title: Phosphate additives
links.effect: Phosphorus from additives is absorbed almost completely. For people with chronic kidney disease, high phosphate intake is linked with faster disease progression and heart problems.
links.source: EFSA — Re-evaluation of phosphates as food additives (2019)

links.title: Caffeine
links.effect: Too much caffeine can cause poor sleep, anxiety and a fast heartbeat. Children are more sensitive, and high intake in pregnancy is linked with lower birth weight.
links.source: EFSA — Scientific opinion on the safety of caffeine (2015)
